author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The General's Old Map
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
I recognized the map before I understood why Iroh had gone quiet.

It had arrived from Ba Sing Se in a flat wooden case, wrapped in oilcloth. The sender was a retired quartermaster who had heard that Moonroot Archive was collecting documents about dangerous crossings and old roads. He had included a note asking whether the archive wanted the map for its historical collection.

Iroh opened the case in the back room of the Jasmine Dragon.

The parchment smelled of dust and cedar. Faded lines marked rivers, supply roads, and a section of city wall drawn with the careful indifference of someone who had never lived beneath it.

The title was written in Fire Nation military script.

Iroh did not touch the page.

"Would you like me to put it away?" I asked.

"Not yet."

I waited.

He took off his reading glasses, polished them with a cloth, put them on again, and looked at the map.

"Do you know what this is?"

"An old siege plan?"

"An old route into a city that did not invite us."

My stomach tightened.

He spoke with the even precision I associated with his old command voice, the one he used when a teapot was burning and someone needed clear instructions. There was no anger in it. That made the words harder to hear.

"The marks indicate where my army expected resistance to weaken. Supply depots. Water routes. Places where we believed families would run if the fighting reached the streets."

I had read enough history to know what a siege meant. I had never seen it laid out in ink by a person I loved.

"Did you draw it?"

"Some of it."

He pointed to a section near the outer wall. His fingertip stopped short of the parchment.

"I ordered a survey there."

I sat on the bench beside him, leaving room between us.

"Do you want to tell me about it?"

He looked at me.

"I do not know whether I deserve the comfort of telling you."

"That's not the question."

He closed his eyes for a moment.

"Then yes. Some of it."

He told me about the cold mornings before the attack, the officers who waited for numbers, the people who tried to turn uncertainty into confidence because soldiers needed something to believe. He told me about seeing a damaged canal and thinking of it only as a tactical weakness. He did not call his younger self foolish. He called him responsible.

I had never heard him say the word with so much weight.

"People lived beside that canal," he said. "I knew they did. I still marked it."

I watched his hand.

"I can't tell you that it was all right," I said.

"I would not ask you to."

"Was the survey used?"

"Not in the way we planned." His jaw worked. "Another decision changed the course of the siege. But the fact that a plan was not carried out does not make the intention harmless."

Outside the tea shop, someone laughed. A customer called for more hot water. The world continued in the particular, ordinary way it always did when someone was remembering what it cost to live through history.

Iroh turned to the note from the quartermaster.

"The archive might display it."

"Maybe. With context."

"Would you object?"

"I'd want to know who gets to tell the story beside it."

He looked toward the window.

"The people who endured the siege."

"Yes."

He nodded slowly.

We took the map to Moonroot after closing.

Severus was at the worktable with a small magnifying glass and a stack of damaged ledgers. He glanced at the wooden case.

"Another document requiring repair?"

"Perhaps," Iroh said. "And a warning."

Severus opened the case and read the title.

His face did not soften. He knew enough about wars to understand that a plan could be both technically detailed and morally abhorrent.

"An archive may preserve a document without endorsing its contents," he said.

"Will you preserve mine?" Iroh asked.

"If we can explain what it is and why it matters."

Neri joined us with the arrival ledger. They suggested a public exhibit about old routes and the Closed Bells, combining documents from multiple worlds.

Iroh shook his head.

"No. Not yet. The siege is not the Lanternweald's history to turn into a convenient parable. The people whose homes appear on that paper must be able to determine how it is presented."

Severus looked up.

"For once, I agree entirely."

I tried to hide my smile.

Neri accepted the correction.

We made a temporary catalog entry with restricted public display and a note requesting historical testimony from Ba Sing Se scholars. Iroh wrote the accession description himself, choosing words that did not conceal his role.

When it was finished, he stared at the page.

"That is a better account than I was prepared to give."

"It isn't complete," I said.

"No."

"Then it can be revised when the people who lived through it speak."

He nodded.

We returned to Jasmine Steps after dark. The last lanterns glowed along the terrace. A little water had collected in a crack beside the stairs. Iroh stepped around it without thinking, then stopped.

"Look," he said.

I followed his gaze.

The rainwater had found the shallowest path down the stone, carrying a few stray petals from the garden. It was nothing like the river on the old map, but the shape was familiar.

"I saw a water route and thought of a weakness," he said. "You see it and think of the people who need to walk safely."

"I also think somebody should repair the step."

He smiled, tired but real.

"You have an inconvenient gift for returning us to work."

"I'm not here to redeem the past with a staircase."

"No." He took my hand. "Nor should you be."

We sat on the balcony outside the tea room. The air smelled of jasmine and stone warmed by the day. Iroh brought a blanket, then asked before settling it around my shoulders.

I leaned against him.

"I don't need you to tell me I'm good," he said after a while.

"Then I won't."

"But I am grateful you can love me without pretending there is nothing to answer for."

I pressed my cheek against his sleeve. There was a trace of tea on the fabric, and the soft scratch of its weave against my skin.

"I love the person sitting here," I said. "And I expect him to tell the truth."

He held me closer.

"That sounds difficult."

"It is."

"Then perhaps tomorrow I will make us a particularly strong tea."

"With mountain mint?"

"If you insist."

I turned toward him. He watched my face, then met me halfway for a slow kiss that left both of us quiet.

Later we took the blanket inside and closed the balcony doors against the rain. There was no grand promise, no claim that a confession had erased a war. Only warmth, the relief of being able to speak, and the work that would remain in the morning.

At breakfast, Iroh set the wooden case by the door, ready to return it to the archive.

The map was still old. The ink was still there.

Now the catalog would have room for more than the general's account.
